full_judgment: 3. Admittedly, plot No. 122 did not belong to either of the contending parties and plot No. 322 and not plot No. 122 in the normal course of things ought to have been included in the hotchpot. Evidently it was a mistake in inserting plot No. 122 in place of plot No. 322 and the report of the Advocate Commissioner also confirmed it. A court can review or modify its orders while it is still seized of a case and retains jurisdiction. I do not find any bar under section 151, C.P.C. to entertain an application for correcting a mistake nor are the hands of court in any way fettered in making such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice. Moreover, Section 152, C.P.C. empowers the court to correct clerical or arithmetical mistakes or errors arising from any accidental slip or omission either on its own motion or on the application of the parties. The section does not necessarily refer to accidental slip or omission of the court itself or its ministerial officer. Where a mistake has crept into the description of an item of property in the plaint schedule and the mistake has been carried over in the decree, the court certainly has powers to correct the error in the decree. If the court is satisfied that the mistake made by the parties in the pleadings is an accidental slip or omission or is due to in advertence and it is so palpable that nobody can possibly have any doubt as to what the parties meant, I do not see why the court cannot set it right. Even if section 151, C.P.C. is not applicable in a case like the present one, the court still has ample powers under section 152, C.P.C. to correct a mistake. A court competent to grant the requisite relief should not reject an application on the ground of maintainability only because relief has been sought under a wrong provision of law. The view I have taken finds support from the decisions in the case of Mohabir Prasad Chowdhury and ors. Vs. Chandra Sekhor Sahi reported in 19 C.W.N. page 1021 and the case of Bela Debi Vs. Ban Behary Roy reported in AIR 1952 Cal. 86. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, I find that the impugned order cannot be sustained and is accordingly set aside. The learned M unsif is directed to hear and dispose of the application on merits.
